items.a: Hi. I'm Thanh, or Albert if that's easier. Ask me anything, or pick a question below.
Thanh Nguyen. Software engineer, systems by day, small tools at night. I like understanding things from the ground up and then making something that runs.
Thanh is my given name. Albert is the one I use when Thanh is hard to say. traceformula is a handle for fun experiments.

Three things. A write-up of cube algebra, the algebra of 3-tensors built the way matrix algebra is built. Piano practice tools that adapt to what you get wrong. And this site: what should a personal page expose once AI agents visit as often as people do?

Matrix algebra has a natural chip, the multiply-accumulate array. Cube algebra replaces the scalar multiply with a short circular convolution, and the whole theory factors through the Fourier transform into a batch of ordinary matrix algebras. That is the hardware thesis: a transform, then a batch of matmuls.

items.q: What math do you work on?
items.a: The tensor write-up is the clearest example: taking a research literature and assembling it into one development, with proofs at textbook level and the computational primitive visible at every step.

items.q: Tell me about the piano tools
items.a: I started piano as an adult and could not find drills I liked, so I built them: an ear trainer, a note reader, a fingering coach, and 290 tunes to play by ear. Whatever you miss comes back more often. Plain HTML, works offline on a phone.

items.q: What is Sophia & Ethan's Math Quest?
items.a: A free math game for kids aged 10 to 15 and up, in Vietnamese and English. You walk a hero through a world, battle monsters by solving problems, and climb 12 realms. There are 1,677 problems, many with a drawing, and the boss puzzles end in an animated proof.

items.q: How do you think learning should work?
items.a: Learning should be fun and it should include struggle. The fun is what brings a kid back, and the struggle is where the learning happens. So in my math game a hint costs a star, and the full solution stays hidden until you have tried and missed twice.

Yes. 600 original contest-style puzzles across 40 realms, in four levels: Kangaroo style for ages 10 to 11, MATHCOUNTS and AMC 8 for 12 to 13, AMC 10 for 14 to 15, and AMC 12, AIME and olympiad style after that. Each has a chain of hints and a full solution.

items.q: Is it friendly to AI agents?
items.a: I think a page should say the same thing to a person and to a model fetching raw text. This site has no text on its surface, but it ships about.md, llms.txt, and the exact question bank you are talking to, as qa.json.

Backend systems in Java, Go, C++, Python and Scala at large scale: storage replication, data pipelines, API design, rollouts across regions. Browser-first tools with no framework and no build step. Simulations, interpreters, visualizations. And long-form mathematical writing.

Google, on secure server-side services for YouTube and Search. Amazon, on DynamoDB replication, where a just-in-time log replica cut recovery from 15 minutes to 1. Before that Zocdoc, Uber, and a SaaS startup of my own in Singapore.
B.S. in Computer Science from Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. M.S. in Computer Science from Maharishi University in the United States.
Three to start with: a math game for kids, piano practice tools, and a long write-up on the algebra of 3-tensors.

Mostly things I built to understand them: a Python interpreter in JavaScript, a map of two thousand topics from books and courses I have skimmed, a solar system, a constellation sky, Conway's Game of Life, a LaTeX renderer, and a spaced-repetition app.
Here is everything, one tap each.

I keep the books and courses I have skimmed through as a force-directed graph instead of a list. About two thousand topics. Clusters appear that I would not have named myself.
Lately: distributed systems patterns, matrix calculus for machine learning, time-series forecasting, graph neural networks, and how large language models are built. The map has the full list.

items.q: What do you do for fun?
items.a: In my free time I love learning physics and neuroscience. Chess is my hobby. Sometimes I play badminton, and I love exploring any kind of sport.

items.q: How do we educate the next generation in the age of AI?
items.a: That is a tough question I have been thinking about, and I have no concrete answer yet.

items.q: What is Mai Hoa Dịch Số?
items.a: Mai Hoa Dịch Số, the plum-blossom numerology of Shao Yong. You turn a time or a number into a hexagram. I do not use it to decide anything. I like the arithmetic of it.
Two toys for it: a solar system with tilted elliptical orbits and comets, and a starfield that draws constellations as you watch.
Conway's Game of Life with a brush. Draw with the left button, erase with the right, change the brush size, watch it go.
Java, Go, C++, Python, Scala, JavaScript. For my own tools, plain JavaScript with no framework. It still runs in ten years.

items.q: What do you think about AI?
items.a: I use it daily and I build with it. I am less interested in chat and more in what agents do when they become the visitor, the reader, and the caller of everything we build. That question shaped this site.
